# How a model produces code, and why it can be wrong {#sec-how-models-produce-code}

You have already met the mechanism. The assistant reads everything written so far, scores every possible next token by how likely it is to follow, picks one, appends it, and repeats. Two weeks of predicting expressions and confirming explanations later, it is worth asking the same question about the thing you will lean on most for the rest of the course, which is what the assistant is actually doing when it hands you a function.

## Code is generated the same way sentences are {#sec-code-is-tokens}

The honest answer is that it is doing exactly the same thing, token by token, except the tokens now spell Python instead of English. Ask for a function that translates a codon into an amino acid, and the model does not consult a codon table, does not run anything, and does not check its answer against biology. It produces the most statistically plausible next piece of code, given everything you have said and everything like it in its training, one token at a time, until the function looks finished. First `def`, then a plausible name, then a plausible parameter, then a plausible body, each choice made the same way a plausible next word was chosen when it was writing you a sentence.

It matters that a token is not a line, and not even always a word. The model does not decide on the whole function and then type it out. It commits to one small piece at a time, and each piece it commits to becomes part of the text that the next piece is predicted from. So a function is built forwards, without a plan, in the sense that nothing in the process ever steps back and asks whether the shape being produced will end up doing what was asked. If the first few tokens set off down a path that cannot lead to a correct answer, the remaining tokens will be the most plausible continuation of that path rather than a correction of it. This is one reason a wrong function is usually wrong from early on rather than wrong at the end.

This is also exactly why the output is so good at looking right. Function names, docstrings, tidy indentation, a sensible-looking dictionary of base pairs, sane variable names, a docstring that describes what the function is supposed to do, all of these are things that appear constantly in real and correct code, so the model reproduces that surface fluently and by default. What it has no access to at all is whether the specific logic inside that familiar-looking surface actually computes what the name promises. Nothing in the process of predicting the next plausible token includes running the function and checking the result, because the model is not running anything. It is guessing what correct code tends to look like, not verifying that this particular code is correct.

Notice the uncomfortable consequence. The parts of a function that are easiest for the model to get right, which are the naming, the layout, the docstring, and the general shape, are exactly the parts you use to form your first impression of it. The part it can most easily get wrong, which is the logic, is the part you cannot see without either reading very carefully or running it.

## The shapes that being wrong actually takes {#sec-failure-shapes}

Saying that the assistant is sometimes wrong is too vague to act on. It is more useful to know what wrong tends to look like, because then you know what to look for.

The friendliest failure is code that does not run at all. A misspelled name, a function called with the wrong number of arguments, or a method that does not exist on that type will raise an error the moment you run it, and the interpreter will tell you the line. This is the failure you should hope for, because the machine catches it for you and hands you a precise description of what went wrong.

More dangerous is code that runs perfectly and gives the wrong answer. A slice that is off by one, a loop that stops one iteration early, a comparison that should have been `<=` and is `<`, a reverse complement that reverses but forgets to complement. Nothing raises an error, the function returns a value of the right type, and only the value itself is wrong. Nothing about the output will announce this. You find it by testing it against a case whose answer you already know.

Then there is code that is right in general and wrong for your data. A function that handles uppercase sequences and silently mishandles lowercase ones, that assumes the sequence length is a multiple of three, that ignores an `N` in a sequencing read, or that assumes a file has no header line. The model produced the version that is most common in its training, which is a reasonable guess about the average case and says nothing about your case.

The most subtle failure is a plausible fact rather than plausible code. A genetic code table with one wrong assignment, a constant with the wrong value, a formula that is nearly the right formula. The code is structurally perfect and the content inside it is quietly incorrect. In molecular biology this is the one to watch hardest, because the tables and constants you will ask about are precisely the kind of thing that appears in text in many slightly different forms.

## Why this will not be patched out {#sec-not-a-bug}

The gap between looking right and being right is not a defect that a future version will fix. It is a direct consequence of how the model works, in the same way that a coin does not become less random with practice. A more capable model will guess better, more often, on harder problems, but guessing better and more often is still guessing. It can still be fluent, confident, and wrong on precisely the case you needed right, and it will hand you that wrong answer with the same tidy formatting it hands you a correct one. There is no warning light. Nothing about the way an assistant presents a wrong function is different from the way it presents a right one, because from the inside, generating one was no different from generating the other.

The word to hold on to for the rest of the term is plausible, and it is doing real work. It is not an insult to the tool, which is often extraordinarily good, and it is not a reason to avoid it. It is a precise description of what its output is, and precise descriptions are what let you build the right habit around them. A plausible answer deserves your attention, and often deserves your trust once you have checked it. It never deserves your trust before you have.

## The one piece of good news {#sec-code-is-checkable}

There is a reason this course is built around code rather than around any of the other things you might ask an assistant for, and it is worth stating plainly, because it is the thing that makes the whole situation manageable.

Code can be run. If you ask the assistant for a summary of a paper, or for an argument, or for advice, checking the answer is slow, effortful, and often requires exactly the expertise you were hoping to borrow. If you ask it for a function, you can feed that function an input whose correct output you already know, and the machine will tell you, in under a second and without any opinion in the matter, whether the function is right about that case. The assistant produces a claim. The interpreter settles it.

That is the entire arrangement this course is training you for, and it explains why the first months are spent on Python rather than on prompting. To run the assistant's function you must be able to read enough of it to know what to feed it. To choose the test case you must understand the problem well enough to know an answer in advance. Neither of those is a prompting skill. Both of them are the ordinary programming understanding you have been building since week one, and they are what turn an unverifiable claim into a checkable one.

#### Exercise {#sec-exercise-palindrome-explain}

`AI: Explainer`

Ask the assistant for a one-line Python function that returns `True` if a DNA strand is a palindrome, meaning it reads the same as its own reverse complement, and `False` otherwise. Before you run anything, read the function and decide, using only your eyes, whether you believe it is right. Then ask the assistant, in a second message, to explain step by step why its own function is correct. Notice that the explanation is generated the same way the code was, one plausible next token at a time, and is not a proof. Does the explanation change how confident you feel, and should it?

#### Exercise {#sec-exercise-known-answer}

`SOLO`

Now settle it without asking anything. Before you run the function, write down by hand two sequences you are certain about, one that is a reverse-complement palindrome and one that is not, and write down the answer you expect for each. Then run the function on both. If it disagrees with you on either, work out which of the two of you is wrong before you change anything, because that is the part of this exercise that is actually hard. Notice how much of the work was choosing the two sequences rather than running the code.

For your logbook this week, describe one moment so far where a fluent-sounding answer from the assistant turned out, on checking, to be wrong, or note that you have not caught one yet, and say what that would tell you about how carefully you have actually been checking. If you did catch one, name which of the failure shapes above it was, because the shapes repeat, and the ones that catch you tend to keep catching you.
